itaconic acid.e: Anagram of aconitic, modelled on German Itaconsäure as an anagram of Aconitsäure (“aconitic acid”), coined by Gustav Crasso (1840).

s.d: a crystalline carboxylic acid; occurs in some fermentations of sugars
(uncountable) One of the isomeric dicarboxylic acids produced by the distillation of citric acid, or as metabolites by microorganisms, CH₂=C(CO₂H)-CH₂CO₂H.

italic.e: Named after the nation of Italy, as it was first used by an Italian printer, Aldo Manuzio, around 1500. Literally Italy + -ic.

s.d: a style of handwriting with the letters slanting to the right
a typeface with letters slanting upward to the right
An oblique handwriting style, such as used by Italian calligraphers of the Renaissance.
x: Spenser uses two different scripts: an Elizabethan secretary hand for English texts, and an italic 'mixed' with secretary graphs for Latin texts […]

s.d: characterized by slanting characters
x: italic characters

s.d: Designed to resemble a handwriting style developed in Italy in the 16th century.
Having letters that slant or lean to the right; oblique.
x: The text was impossible to read: every other word was underlined or in a bold or italic font.

s.d: Of or relating to the Italian peninsula.
Pertaining to a subfamily of the Centum branch of the Indo-European language family, that includes Latin and other languages (as Oscan, Umbrian) spoken by the peoples of ancient Italy
(historical) Pertaining to various peoples that lived in Italy before the establishment of the Roman Empire, or to any of several alphabet systems used by those peoples.
x: There were several Italic alphabets, one being the Etruscan alphabet.

itch.e: From Middle English icche, ȝicche, from Old English ġiċċe (“itch”), from Proto-Germanic *jukjǭ (“itch”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Scots yeuk (“itch, itchiness”), Dutch jeuk (“itch”), German jucken.

s.d: a contagious skin infection caused by the itch mite; characterized by persistent itching and skin irritation
x: he has a bad case of the itch

s.d: a strong restless desire
x: why this urge to travel?

s.d: an irritating cutaneous sensation that produces a desire to scratch
A sensation felt on an area of the skin that causes a person or animal to want to scratch said area.
A constant teasing desire or want.
x: ... it left, however, a bee at his ear and an itch to transfer the buzzer's attentions and tease his darling; for she had betrayed herself as right good game.

s.d: scrape or rub as if to relieve itching
x: Don't scratch your insect bites!

s.d: have or perceive an itch
x: I'm itching — the air is so dry!

s.d: cause to perceive an itch
x: his skin itched

s.d: have a strong desire or urge to do something
x: She is itching to start the project
He is spoiling for a fight

s.d: To feel itchy; to feel a need to be scratched.
To have a constant, teasing urge; to feel strongly motivated; to want or desire something.
x: He started learning to drive and he has been itching for opportunities to practice ever since.

s.d: (colloquial) To scratch or rub so as to relieve an itch.
x: "What makes you suspect him?" Max asked as he itched his neck.
I have to take both shoes and socks off! If I go bare foot I'm ok! I also get itching on my r/palm of my hand. I itch it so much that it's raw!

s.d: whitish mites that attack the skin of humans and other animals
x: itch mites cause scabies

s.d: Sarcoptes scabiei, a parasitic arthropod that burrows into the skin and causes scabies.

itching.e: From Middle English icchynge, ichynge, ycchenge, yecchyng, ʒicchunge (also unassibilated as ʒykynge), equivalent to itch + -ing.

s.d: an irritating cutaneous sensation that produces a desire to scratch
A sensation that itches.
x: Itchings, hitherto unknown, are felt all over the body, and render my skin sometimes painfully tender, sometimes quite benumbed, as if it were dead.

itchy.e: From Middle English *yicchy, *ȝicchi, from Old English ġiċċiġ (“itchy”), equivalent to itch + -y. Cognate with Scots yeukie (“itchy”), West Frisian jokkerich (“itchy”), Dutch jeukachtig and jeukerig (“itchy”).

s.d: nervous and unable to relax
x: a constant fretful stamping of hooves
a restless child

s.d: causing an irritating cutaneous sensation; being affect with an itch
x: he had an itchy toe from the mosquito bite

s.d: Characterized by itching. (of a condition)
x: an itchy rash
Excess, the scrophulous and itchy plague / That seizes first the opulent

s.d: Feeling an itching sensation; feeling a need to be scratched. (of a person, animal or body part)
x: My nose always gets itchy the moment I put on my face mask.

Q. What do you mean by a natural, but sickly delight?
A. I mean such a delight as Itchie people have to scratch, green-sickness Garles to eat coles and chalk, and those in a burning Fever, to drink cold drink.

s.d: Causing an itching sensation.
x: He refuses to wear the new sweater; he says it’s itchy.
the itchy sound, the brisk and scratchy sound, of combing hairs out of a stiff brush

s.d: (figuratively) In a state of agitation; easily alarmed.
x: Casy said softly, “All of ’em’s itchy. Them cops been sayin’ how they’re gonna beat the hell outa us an’ run us outa the county. […]”

1966, Robert A. Heinlein, The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, Chapter 16, in Worlds of If, Volume 16, No. 1, Issue 98, January, 1966, p. 77,
[…] I got itchy wondering whether I could go inside Complex without being nabbed.

s.d: (figuratively) Having a constant, teasing desire (for something, to do something); impatiently eager.
x: Who simply stares and listens / Tongue-tied, while eye nor glistens / Nor brow grows hot and twitchy, / Nor mouth, for a combat itchy, / Quivers with some convincing / Reply
“So I went over to see Miss Huntress and after a lot of finagling around with this itchy-handed house dick I got to see her and we had a chat […]”

s.d: (derogatory, figuratively, obsolete) Feeling or showing a high level of sexual interest.
x: Car[dochia]. That slave in obscene language courted me, / Drew reals out, and would have bought my body, / Diego, from thee. / Die[go]. Is he so itchy? I'll cure him.
what’s all the delight, / That seemes so pleasing to the itchie whorer?

s.d: very strong or irresistible impulse to travel

item.e: From Middle English item, from Latin item (“also; in the same manner”). The present English meaning derives from a usage in lists, where the first entry would begin in primis (“firstly”) or imprimis, and the other entries with item (“also, moreover”). Later, the members of lists were referred to as "items".

s.d: a distinct part that can be specified separately in a group of things that could be enumerated on a list
x: he noticed an item in the New York Times
she had several items on her shopping list

s.d: a small part that can be considered separately from the whole
x: it was perfect in all details

s.d: a whole individual unit; especially when included in a list or collection
x: they reduced the price on many items

s.d: an isolated fact that is considered separately from the whole
x: several of the details are similar
a point of information

s.d: an individual instance of a type of symbol
x: the word ‘error’ contains three tokens of ‘r’

s.d: A distinct physical object.
x: Tweezers are great for manipulating small items.

s.d: An object that can be picked up for later use.
A line of text having a legal or other meaning; a separate particular in an account.
x: the items in a bill
In response to the first item, we deny all wrongdoing.

s.d: A question on a test, which may include its answers.
x: The exam has 100 items, each of which includes a correct response and three distractors.

s.d: A matter for discussion in an agenda.
x: The first item for discussion is the budget for next year's picnic.

s.d: (informal) Two people who are having a romantic or sexual relationship with each other.
x: Jack and Jill are an item.
Are we an item? Girl, quit playin' / "We're just friends," what are you sayin'?

s.d: A short article in a newspaper.
x: an item concerning the weather

s.d: (obsolete) A hint; an innuendo.
x: A secret item was given to some of the bishops […] to absent themselves.

s.d: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter I.
To make a note of.
(used when listing or enumerating items) also
x: a length of chain, item a hook

s.d: likewise
being or characteristic of a single thing or person
x: individual drops of rain
please mark the individual pages

s.d: the act of making a list of items
The system of items available to players and their design and qualities.
x: The itemization in this game is terrible. All the good items are so rare, it gives players no desire to grind at all.

I can't even rhyme in the begin.

iterate.e: The adjective is first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1533, the noun in 1941; partly inherited from Middle English iterat(e) (adjective), partly borrowed from Latin iterātus, perfect passive participle of iterō (“to do something for a second time, repeat”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)) , from iterum (“again”) + -ō. Sporadical participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

s.d: An n-fold self-composition of a function.
x: An important example of such a semigroup in infinite dimensional Hilbert space is the weak operator closed monothetic semigroup generated by a linear operator with equibounded iterates.

s.d: The image of a certain value under such a function.
x: f²(x₀) is the second iterate of x₀ under f.

s.d: to say, state, or perform again
x: She kept reiterating her request

s.d: run or be performed again
x: the function iterates

s.d: To perform or repeat an action on each item in a set.
x: The max() function iterates through the data to find the highest value.

s.d: To perform or repeat an action on the results of each such prior action.
x: In mathematics, an iterated function is a function which is composed with itself, possibly ad infinitum, in a process called iteration.

s.d: (archaic) To utter or do a second time or many times; to repeat.
x: to iterate advice
Nor Eve to iterate / Her former trespass feared.

s.d: To repeat an activity, making incremental changes each time.
x: For NASA and most private aerospace companies, a single crash is a setback that can take years to recover from. SpaceX works more like a Silicon Valley startup, where the goal is to fail quickly and iterate.

s.d: (obsolete) Said or done again; repeated.
(obsolete) Iterated.

iteration.e: From Latin iterātiō, from iterō. Morphologically iterate + -ion.

s.d: (computer science) a single execution of a set of instructions that are to be repeated
x: the solution took hundreds of iterations

s.d: (computer science) executing the same set of instructions a given number of times or until a specified result is obtained
x: the solution is obtained by iteration

s.d: doing or saying again; a repeated performance
(uncountable) A recital or a second performance; a repetition.
(uncountable) A variation or version.
x: The architect drafted several iterations of the floorplan before deciding on his final design.
Still going strong in his ninth decade, Wein celebrates his 88th birthday behind the piano accompanied by the latest iteration of his band, the Newport All-Stars, featuring tenor saxophonist […]

s.d: (uncountable) The use of repetition in a computer program, especially in the form of a loop.
(uncountable) A single repetition of the code within such a repetitive process.
x: The code calculates the appropriate value at each iteration.

s.d: the aspect of the verb that expresses the repetition of an action
A verb showing the iterative aspect.
marked by iteration
Of a procedure that involves repetition of steps (iteration) to achieve the desired outcome; in computing this may involve a mechanism such as a loop.
Expressive of an action that is repeated with frequency.
the aspect of the verb that expresses the repetition of an action
(uncountable) A subclass of imperfective verbs that denote a continuously repeated action. An example in English would be the iterative verb sniffle, as opposed to the noniterative sniff.

itinerant.e:
From Late Latin itinerantem, present active participle of itineror (“travel”), from itiner-.
By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ant.

s.d: a laborer who moves from place to place as demanded by employment
x: itinerant traders

s.d: One who travels from place to place.
(Ireland) A member of the Travelling Community, whether settled or not.
traveling from place to place to work
x: itinerant labor
an itinerant judge

s.d: Habitually travelling from place to place.
x: an itinerant preacher or peddler
The king's own courts were then itinerant, being kept in the king's palace, and removing with his household in those royal progresses which he continually made.

itinerary.e: From Middle English itinerarie, from Latin itinerārium (“an account of a journey, a road-book”), from iter (“a way, journey”). By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ary.

s.d: an established line of travel or access
a guidebook for travelers
a proposed route of travel
A written schedule of activities for a vacation or road trip.
An account or record of a journey.
A guidebook for travellers.
Itinerant; travelling from place to place; done on a journey.
x: It were rather an itinerary circuit of justice than a progress.

s.d: travel from place to place, as for work
x: an itinerating merchant

s.d: To travel from place to place, especially to preach or lecture.

itineration.e: From itinerate + -ion, ultimately borrowed from Medieval Latin itinerātiō, from itineror (“travel”), from itiner-.

s.d: journeying from place to place preaching or lecturing; a preaching tour or lecturing tour
(formal, uncountable) A travelling around.
x: In company with William I made several interesting itinerations on the hills during the last cold season, an account of which has been sent home to the Board; also a tour of upwards of 350 miles on the plains […]

itraconazole.e: Probably from itra- (“alteration of tria(zole)”) + -conazole (“miconazole derivative”).

s.d: an oral antifungal drug (trade name Sporanox) taken for cases of fungal nail disease
(uncountable) A particular triazole antifungal agent (trademark Sporanox) that may be given orally or intravenously especially to treat blastomycosis and histoplasmosis.

itsy-bitsy.e: From itty (baby-talk form of little) and/or bitsy.

s.d: A very small thing; something tiny or insignificant.
(used informally) little or tiny
x: a wee tot

s.d: (colloquial, humorous) Very small; minuscule.
x: The itsy-bitsy spider climbed up the water spout.
She wore an itsy-bitsy teeny-weeny yellow polka-dot bikini.

s.d: (used informally) little or tiny
x: a wee tot
